extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and students studying Gabriel García Márquez-style magical realism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing/assessing Latin American-style magical realism in fiction, with emphasis on narrative tone, treatment of the supernatural, and stylistic devices associated with García Márquez.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadpan magical (omniscient narrator's tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: The omniscient narrator reports impossible events with deadpan objectivity. Extraordinary details are rendered with the same matter-of-factness as ordinary ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: levitation described in the same tone as sweeping the floor. Evaluative note from the page: 'The deadpan narrator's tone is unbroken across natural and supernatural.' Maintain identical narrative register for natural and supernatural events; avoid tonal shifts that single out the magical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial reticence (do not explain the magical)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator does not explain the magical. No marvelling, no asides, no signaling of the unusual; the text gives the reader no permission to question the magical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: avoid explicit explanation, commentary, or incredulous framing by the narrator or other characters. The page notes García Márquez learned this from his grandmother, whose tone never varied whether telling about ghosts or prices — model narration on that steadiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerically specific exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyperbole gains reality when it is precise — specific, numeric exaggeration reads more factual than vague hyperbole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: Colonel Aureliano Buendía's 'thirty-two armed uprisings, all of which he lost'; the rainstorm that lasts 'four years, eleven months, and two days'; 'a hundred years of solitude.' Anti-pattern: vague hyperbole ('many years,' 'countless uprisings') which reads nebulous rather than veridical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Native beliefs as knowledge, not folklore
rubrics_metrics.description: Native and popular beliefs (ghosts, premonitions, miracles) are treated as valid knowledge within the narrative rather than exotic decoration or folklore to be explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrator and characters share the same epistemology: supernatural occurrences are integrated into what counts as knowledge in the story world. This technique resists colonial framing that measures against Western rationality; avoid othering or exoticizing beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saturation of the magical
rubrics_metrics.description: Magical events are not rare punctuations; they saturate the world so strangeness becomes the background texture of the setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worldbuilding guidance: populate the setting (e.g., Macondo) with constant, recurring strangeness rather than single spectacular incidents. The goal is woven texture rather than isolated spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensory richness coupled with restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions are sensory-rich (smells, colors, weather, fruit) while the narrator's emotional commentary is restrained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show through vivid sensory detail but do not tell the reader how to feel; let the sensory data carry emotional weight. The page frames this as 'sensory overload coupled with restraint' — abundant detail without emotive authorial intrusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cyclical time (nonlinear/recursive temporality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative frequently uses cyclical or recursive time: names recur across generations, events rhyme, and history repeats rather than strictly linear progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural device: permit events and motifs to recur and echo across the text. The page contrasts this with linear narrative as a Western imposition; use repetition and recursion to create mythic temporality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary inheritance and technique models (Faulkner and Borges)
rubrics_metrics.description: García Márquez's craft draws on Faulkner (making a place into a cosmos) and Borges (deadpan handling of impossibilities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: consider building a mythic, self-contained place (à la Faulkner's Yoknapatawpha) and adopt Borges-like tonal restraint when introducing the impossible. Use these antecedents as technical models rather than direct content templates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success checklist for magical realism
rubrics_metrics.description: A magical-realist work succeeds when several conditions are met simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pulling together the page's evaluative bullets: (a) The deadpan narrator's tone is unbroken across natural and supernatural; (b) Hyperbole is numerically specific; (c) Magical events arise from the same epistemology as ordinary events (not exoticized); (d) Native beliefs operate as knowledge, not primitivism to be explained; (e) Sensory description is rich without emotional commentary; (f) The world is saturated with strangeness, not punctuated by it. Use this list as an integrated checklist when assessing a text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure modes (signs a text is not successful magical realism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common ways magical realism can fail are explicitly noted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure indicators listed on the page: the narrator 'winks' or signals the magical as remarkable; hyperbole is vague rather than precise; beliefs are framed as quaint or exotic; the work reads as fantasy rather than magical realism (the magical becomes the rule rather than a woven texture). When any of these occur, the text may collapse into fantasy, satire, or exoticism rather than magical realism.
